chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Hilal, from Uqba ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding

a man who bought goods from a man and made the sale binding, except that he left the goods with the seller and did not take possession of it, saying, 'I will come to you tomorrow, God willing.' Then the goods were stolen. Whose wealth would that be? He said: 'From the wealth of the owner of the goods, which are in his house, until the goods are taken possession of and removed from his house. So when they are removed from his house, the buyer is liable for their value until he returns their money to him.'
ai.seo_question: Who bears the risk of loss if goods are sold but not yet taken by the buyer?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *daman* (liability) in sales, emphasizing that physical possession (*qabd*) is the decisive factor for transferring risk, rather than the mere completion of the contract. It highlights the scholarly distinction between the seller retaining custody of the goods in their own home versus the buyer taking them into their sphere of control, ensuring fairness in cases of accidental loss or theft. This ruling underscores the practical application of possession as the threshold for financial responsibility in Islamic commercial jurisprudence.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Al Husayn, from Muhammad Bin Abdullah Bin Hilal, from Uqba Bin Khalid,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> regarding a man who buys some goods from a man and makes it binding apart from that he leave the goods with him and does not take possession of it, saying, ‘I will come to you tomorrow, Allah<sup>saww</sup> Willing’. So the goods get stolen. From whose wealth would that happen to be (stolen)?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘From the wealth of the owner of the goods which are in his house until the goods are taken possession of, and it goes out from his house. So when it goes out from his house, so the buyer is responsible for his right until he return his wealth back to him’.
en.sarwar: 12. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah ibn Hilal from ‘Uqbah ibn abu Khalid who has said the following: “This is concerning my question before abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about

the case of a man who purchases something from a man and makes a binding deal and then leaving the merchandise with him without taking possession saying, Tomorrow, by the will of Allah, I will come back.’ Someone steals the merchandise. Whose property is it considered? He (the Imam) replied, Tt is the property of the seller until the buyer takes possession and it is taken away from the seller’s house. When this happens the buyer is responsible until he returns it back to the seller.’”
